Hi Sam,

 

A few things.

 

First, those wiki pages are rather outdated: geomorph contains output for quite a few items which previously required post-hoc calculations. These additions make some Wiki pages and their calculations superfluous.

 

One example is extracting group means. This is obtained in several ways in geomorph, but one is as part of the output in advanced.procD.lm.  For instance running:

 

Myres<-advanced.procD.lm(f1=shape~groups, f2=~1, groups = groups, data = myGDF)

Myres$LS.means

 

This will run the model, and the output $LS.means contains the least squares means for the groups. Note that the approach is general and can obtain LS means for models with covariates (see help file).

 

As to your measurement error issue, as stated in the Wiki, the repeatability equation used was for the simple case of 2 replicates from a single set of images. You have a more complex design, and having more complex input data may require altering these equation to correspond with correct MS terms from the linear model.

 

To fully appreciate how to implement more general measurement analyses (multiple individuals, multiple photos, multiple measurements, etc.), I first recommend a careful reading of Chapter 9 of Zelditch et al., as well as the paper by Arnqvist and Martensson 1998 (among others).  Here the expected mean squares are discussed, so one can learn how to extract the correct MS components from the factorial anova table and perform the repeatability analysis.

 

Best,

 

Dean

Hi Sam,

It is quite unsurprising that you will get negative values with your math because you are subtracting larger MS values from smaller ones.  I’m not sure what you are attempting to do.  Maybe Emma will want to chime in about her original example but if I understood it correctly, the point was to examine (as a reduction from 100%) the amount of variation added by having repeated versions of individuals digitized.  The model has two sources: individuals and residuals (replication).  Her example works IF AND ONLY IF the variation among individuals exceeds the variation within individuals.  If measurement error exceeds inter-individual variation, then the repeatability value she suggested could be negative.  To me, this means you have so much measurement error that any other inference might be foolhardy to make.  

But none of the models you are showing us here looks like the one she made.  She also mentioned at the end of her discussion that a factorial model can be used when there are multiple photos and multiple digitizations for each photo.  She did not suggest to try to manipulate MS values like you have if this is the case.  

It looks to me that you are combining different topics (model types) in attempting to find results.

Mike

It is quite unsurprising that you will get negative values with your math because you are subtracting larger MS values from smaller ones.  I’m not sure what you are attempting to do.  Maybe Emma will want to chime in about her original example but if I understood it correctly, the point was to examine (as a reduction from 100%) the amount of variation added by having repeated versions of individuals digitized.  The model has two sources: individuals and residuals (replication).  Her example works IF AND ONLY IF the variation among individuals exceeds the variation within individuals.  If measurement error exceeds inter-individual variation, then the repeatability value she suggested could be negative.  To me, this means you have so much measurement error that any other inference might be foolhardy to make.  

But none of the models you are showing us here looks like the one she made.  She also mentioned at the end of her discussion that a factorial model can be used when there are multiple photos and multiple digitizations for each photo.  She did not suggest to try to manipulate MS values like you have if this is the case.  

It looks to me that you are combining different topics (model types) in attempting to find results.
Mike

I see a couple of confusing things here.  First, Emma had indicated before (in the tutorial) to use a factorial model.  You model is not a factorial model, as it does not have Ind and Photo as factors; it has only the interaction.  Emma gave the calculation of repeatability - which you are trying to force on this model despite her using it on a different model, ~ Ind - but she did not say that the formula she gave for the simpler model could just be copied and used again on this model.  You are making that assumption and now concluding that you have 5% repeatability (95% measurement error?).  I believe this is not correct.  Finally, with a factorial model, there would be different possible measurements like this, comparing individuals to photos and photos to replicate digitizations on photos.

Hi Sam,

 

A few things.

 

First, those wiki pages are rather outdated: geomorph contains output for quite a few items which previously required post-hoc calculations. These additions make some Wiki pages and their calculations superfluous.

 

One example is extracting group means. This is obtained in several ways in geomorph, but one is as part of the output in advanced.procD.lm.  For instance running:

 

Myres<-advanced.procD.lm(f1=shape~groups, f2=~1, groups = groups, data = myGDF)

Myres$LS.means

 

This will run the model, and the output $LS.means contains the least squares means for the groups. Note that the approach is general and can obtain LS means for models with covariates (see help file).

 

As to your measurement error issue, as stated in the Wiki, the repeatability equation used was for the simple case of 2 replicates from a single set of images. You have a more complex design, and having more complex input data may require altering these equation to correspond with correct MS terms from the linear model.

 

To fully appreciate how to implement more general measurement analyses (multiple individuals, multiple photos, multiple measurements, etc.), I first recommend a careful reading of Chapter 9 of Zelditch et al., as well as the paper by Arnqvist and Martensson 1998 (among others).  Here the expected mean squares are discussed, so one can learn how to extract the correct MS components from the factorial anova table and perform the repeatability analysis.

 

Best,

It is quite unsurprising that you will get negative values with your math because you are subtracting larger MS values from smaller ones.  I’m not sure what you are attempting to do.  Maybe Emma will want to chime in about her original example but if I understood it correctly, the point was to examine (as a reduction from 100%) the amount of variation added by having repeated versions of individuals digitized.  The model has two sources: individuals and residuals (replication).  Her example works IF AND ONLY IF the variation among individuals exceeds the variation within individuals.  If measurement error exceeds inter-individual variation, then the repeatability value she suggested could be negative.  To me, this means you have so much measurement error that any other inference might be foolhardy to make.  

 

But none of the models you are showing us here looks like the one she made.  She also mentioned at the end of her discussion that a factorial model can be used when there are multiple photos and multiple digitizations for each photo.  She did not suggest to try to manipulate MS values like you have if this is the case.  

 

It looks to me that you are combining different topics (model types) in attempting to find results.
Mike
